title: Slide-writing skill
description: Installs the writing-slides Agent Skill under .agents/skills: how to turn material into a talk of one-idea slides with sentence headlines, visual evidence, builds, code that fits and steps through, and speaker notes, with this deck's syntax and measured limits, its failure modes, and pnpm check followed by a look at every slide, next to the general skills the skills patch provides.

content: name: writing-slides

description: Writes and revises talks in a deck made from the slides template (slides.mdx), turning a topic, outline, article or README into a narrative of one-idea slides with sentence headlines, visual evidence instead of bullet lists, builds for sequences, code that fits the frame and steps through with highlights, diffs and magic moves, and speaker notes that carry the detail, then checks every slide with pnpm check before finishing. Use when asked to write, outline, restructure, shorten, review, fix or brand a talk, presentation, deck or slides.mdx, including requests such as "add a slide about X", "turn this post into a 20-minute talk" or "the code on slide 7 does not fit". Not for .pptx, Keynote, Slidev or Marp decks. Load mermaid-diagrams alongside it for diagram syntax, and hand the prose of speaker notes to humanizer.
# Writing slides

**A slide is what the audience reads while the speaker talks; everything else goes in `<Notes>`.** Most bad decks are the speaker's script projected on a wall, and every rule below follows from not doing that.

**Check that the deck comes from the slides template.** `slides.mdx` at the root with `plugins/remark-slides.ts` next to it says so. Without them the syntax here does not apply: say which kind of deck it is and apply only the design rules. The deck's own syntax is documented in its `README.md`, which wins where it and this skill disagree.
## Start from the talk, not the slides
Before writing a slide, settle four things, from the request and the material, and state any you had to assume:
- **The audience**, and what they already know.
- **The length.** Budget about one content slide per minute, and plan for 80% of the slot.
- **The big idea**, one sentence with a verb and a stake: what the audience should remember if they remember nothing else. Every slide supports it, and material that does not is cut.
- **The arc**: the problem and the promise in the first two or three slides, the argument, and a last slide that restates the big idea.

The deck a project starts with includes a tour of the template from `chapters/tour.mdx`: a real talk replaces that `<Include>` in `slides.mdx` with its own slides, and deletes `chapters/tour.mdx`, `chapters/example.mdx` and `snippets/counter.ts` once nothing uses them. Never write the talk into the tour's files: `weft update` changes them.

Then **write every headline first, in order, and read them as a paragraph.** If they do not make the argument on their own, no slide body will fix it. No agenda before the problem is stated, and no "Questions?" or "Thank you" as the last slide; the takeaway stays up during questions. `references/talk-structure.md` has the arc, signposting and timing in detail: read it when outlining a new talk or restructuring one.
## The headline is the claim

Every content slide's `##` is a full sentence stating what the slide shows, in at most two lines: about 90 characters at `##`, 70 at `#`. A topic label makes the audience work out the point; a sentence tells them, and they remember it (79% against 69% correct in Alley's study). A question headline does worse still, unless a later step answers it.
```mdx
## Results                                              ← a label
## Caching cut p99 latency from 800 ms to 120 ms        ← the claim
`<Cover>`, `<Section>`, `<Statement>` and `<Quote>` are exempt: their content is the headline. Never put a sentence headline inside a `<Columns>` cell, where 22 characters fit on a line.
## Evidence, not bullets

The body shows why the headline is true: code, a diagram, an image, a table, one number as a `<Stat value label>`, or two things side by side in `<Columns>`. Not a list of the things you will say. When a sentence has to sit beside the code or the image it is about, give the evidence the wider column and centre both: `<Columns widths="3:2" align="center">`.
- **About 20 visible words on a content slide**, counting the headline and body text but not code or notes. At 33 or more the audience reads instead of listening.
- **A list has at most four items**, each at most two lines, and never stands alone under a headline.
- **The sentences you will say go in `<Notes>`**, as cues, not a script: the audience cannot read and listen at once.
- **Compare on one slide**, never across two: `<Columns>`, a `diff`, a magic move.
- **Label the thing itself.** No legend, no "see left", no "as shown below".
Before, the speaker's script on the canvas:
```mdx
## Retries
- We retry failed requests up to 5 times
- Retries use exponential backoff starting at 100 ms
- Without jitter, clients retry at the same moment
- This caused the outage on 12 March
- Adding full jitter spreads retries out
- p99 recovery time dropped from 14 min to 90 s
After, the claim, the change as evidence, and the detail in notes:
````mdx
## Full jitter cut outage recovery from 14 minutes to 90 seconds
```ts diff title="src/retry.ts"
const base = 100 * 2 ** attempt
-await sleep(base)
+await sleep(Math.random() * base)
<Notes>
- 5 retries, exponential backoff from 100 ms
- 12 March: every client retried in lockstep and the database never recovered
- Source for 14 min to 90 s: the incident review
</Notes>
Every number, date, version and quotation on a slide comes from the user's material, with its source in that slide's notes. Never invent a figure to make a slide land.
## Builds

`<Steps>` reveals a list item by item and `<Step>` reveals one block; highlight steps and magic moves build code. **Build a graphic or code as you talk about its parts; do not drip-feed text bullets** unless the last one is a punch line. Keep a text build to four items.

The print view and the overview show every slide fully revealed, so **the last step of a slide must make sense on its own**: a highlight sequence ends on `all`, which also leaves folds shut, and a magic move's last version is the one worth printing.
## Code
Read `references/code-slides.md` before writing or editing any slide with code: the fence options, the measured limits and the patterns for showing change. The rules that decide most code slides:
- **One idea per code slide, and the `##` says what the code does or proves.**

- **It fits at full size.** At 15 px a line holds 88 characters across the slide, 39 in a `<Columns>` cell, and 48 in the wide cell of `widths="3:2"` (84, 35 and 43 with `lineNumbers`). A block under a one-line headline holds 13 lines, 11 with `title=`; under a two-line headline, 12 and 10. Code that does not fit is shrunk to fit, down to 80%, and `pnpm check` warns about it: **treat that warning as a failure** and cut, split or add `maxLines`.

- **Cut what is not the point**, imports, boilerplate and error handling included, and mark the gap with `// …`. Say in the notes when shown code would not compile as is. Where the code must stay whole, fold instead: `fold={4-11}` hides those lines behind one line until a step highlights inside them.
- **Show change as change**: a `diff`, `diff split` or a magic move, never two full listings.
- **Prefer real code**: `file="./snippets/…"` reads it from a file that `pnpm typecheck` compiles.
## Diagrams

A `mermaid` fence in the deck becomes an SVG when it builds, so load `mermaid-diagrams` for the syntax and its readability rules. Its rule against diagrams in files of their own is written for GitHub; here the fence goes in `slides.mdx` like any other. On a 16:9 slide keep to about six nodes, prefer `flowchart LR`, and keep labels to a word or two: the build warns when a diagram is too wide, and the check warns when its labels end up under 18 px.
## Legibility
The canvas is 960 × 540 and scales to the screen, so a canvas pixel is a point on a standard PowerPoint slide, and accessibility guidance applies directly.
- **Nothing the audience must read is under 18 px, except code at 15 px.** Body text is 20 px, tables and callouts 18 px. No `text-sm` or `text-xs` on content, and no `class="text-sm"` on a fence.
- **Contrast**: no `text-muted-foreground/70` or lighter on content, and nothing important only in a code comment, which is 3.9:1 in the dark theme.
- **Colour never carries meaning alone**: the deck is shown in light and dark, and printed.
- **Never hide overflow.** No `overflow-hidden`, `max-h-*`, `scale-*`, `zoom` or smaller text added to make a slide pass. Split the slide.
Read `references/brand.md` when a deck must follow a brand or a logo: where the colours, fonts and logo go, and how much of them a slide can carry.
## MDX traps
`slides.mdx` is MDX, not Markdown, and one mistake can blank the whole deck:
- A literal `{` or `}` in prose is JavaScript: write `\{`, or put it in inline code. A bare `{word}` compiles, then throws in the browser.

- Comments are `{/* … */}`, never ``. A `<` before a digit breaks the parse: write "under 100 ms". `
` must be `
`, and links are `[text](url)`, never ``.
- Markdown inside a component needs blank lines around it, or it stays one inline line.

- `---` needs a blank line above it. Right under a line of text it underlines that line into a `##` heading, and the slide or the `<Columns>` does not split; the build warns `"---" right under "…" makes it a heading`.
## Check, then look
These commands are for you; none of them belong in a slide or its notes.

1. **Run `pnpm check`.** It type-checks the slides (a wrong prop or a misspelt component is an error), builds, renders every step of every slide, fails on content that runs off a slide or out of a code frame at any step, warns about code or a diagram shrunk to fit, and writes an image of every slide to `.tmp/export/`. Fix every failure and every warning.

2. **Look at every image in `.tmp/export/` as the audience would.** Read the headlines in order first, then each slide against the rules above. A passing check is not a good talk. An author reviewing their own slides explains the problems away, so hand this to a fresh context where you can: a subagent given the images, the headlines in order and the checklist below, asked to list the problems on each slide. It judges; measuring sizes and overflow is the check's job. Where no subagent can run, or one does not report, review in two passes yourself: write down every problem on every slide first, then fix them.
3. **Fix, rerun, and stop after a clean pass.**
`references/failure-modes.md` lists each failure with a test that finds it and the fix: read it when reviewing a deck, or when the check or the look finds something you cannot place.
## When rules collide
1. **The audience can read it** beats fitting the content on one slide: split the slide, never shrink the text.
2. **One idea per slide** beats the slide count: cut an idea from the talk before packing two onto a slide.
3. **The user's explicit instruction** beats the style rules here, but not legibility or the check; say what you kept against the guidance and why it matters.
4. **The fully revealed slide makes sense** beats a clever build.
## Before you finish
- The big idea is one sentence, and the headlines read in order make the argument.
- Every content slide's `##` is a sentence of at most two lines.
- No content slide is a headline and a list, and no list has more than four items.
- Every content slide has `<Notes>`, and no sentence of the notes is on the slide.
- Every figure on a slide comes from the user's material, with its source in the notes.
- Code fits at full size, ends its highlights on `all`, and shows change as change.
- Nothing the audience must read is under 18 px, or 15 px for code.
- `pnpm check` passed with no warnings, and every image in `.tmp/export/` was looked at.
- The last slide is the takeaway, not "Questions?".
- The prose in the notes went through `humanizer`.
## Sources
Read 2026-09-28; check them before relying on a number, since guidance moves.

- Garner and Alley, "How the design of presentation slides affects audience comprehension", *International Journal of Engineering Education* 29(6), 2013: sentence headlines with visual evidence against topic headlines with bullets, 21 against 42 words a slide.
- Alley, Schreiber, Ramsdell and Muffo, "How the design of headlines in presentation slides affects audience retention", *Technical Communication* 53(2), 2006.
- Alley and Neeley, "Rethinking the design of presentation slides", *Technical Communication* 52(4), 2005.

- Mayer and Fiorella, "Principles for reducing extraneous processing in multimedia learning", *Cambridge Handbook of Multimedia Learning*, 2014: coherence, redundancy, spatial and temporal contiguity.
- Kosslyn, Kievit, Russell and Shephard, "PowerPoint presentation flaws and failures", *Frontiers in Psychology* 3:230, 2012.
- Microsoft, "Make your PowerPoint presentations accessible", and W3C, WCAG 2.2 success criteria 1.4.3 and 1.4.11: 18 pt, 4.5:1 and 3:1.
- Simon Peyton Jones, "How to give a great research talk"; Nancy Duarte, *Resonate* and *Slidedocs*; Patrick Winston, "How to Speak", MIT OpenCourseWare.

# A deck in a brand's colours

Where a brand goes in this deck, and how much of it a slide can carry. A brand is there to be recognised, not to fill the slides: the audience should know whose talk it is from the first slide and then look at the evidence.
## Contents
- Where it goes
- The logo
- Colour
- Contrast
- Checking it
## Where it goes

- **Colours** are the tokens in `src/index.css`, once in `:root` and once in `.dark`: `--primary` is the brand colour and `--primary-foreground` the text on it; `--foreground` and `--muted-foreground` take the brand's text greys, if it has them; `--ring` and `--chart-1` to `--chart-5` usually follow the primary. The code highlight, `<Stat>` numbers and the cover's glow take the primary; diagrams take the text colours and the chart tokens.
- **Full slides in the brand colour** are `<Cover variant="primary">`, and the same on `<Section>`, `<Statement>` and `<Quote>`. Never rebuild them with colour classes by hand.

- **Fonts** come from an `@fontsource` package imported in `src/index.css`, with `--font-sans` or `--font-heading` pointing at it. Keep the deck's font when the brand's is not licensed for the web; a close free face beats a missing one.
- **Logo files** go in `public/`, referenced without a leading slash, such as `logo.svg`.
## The logo
**Use the brand's own files**, from its brand guide, press kit or website, never a redrawing. When only a bitmap exists, trace it to SVG and compare the two side by side at the size they will show.

**Show it on the cover and the last slide, not on every slide.** A logo in the corner of every slide is decoration the audience stops seeing, and it takes room from the evidence (Mayer and Fiorella's coherence principle). Keep the clear space the brand asks for, and never stretch, recolour or add an effect the brand does not use itself.
## Colour

**The brand colour marks what matters, sparingly**: the cover, section slides, the number on a `<Stat>`, the highlight in code. Emphasis works when there is little of it (Mayer and Fiorella's signalling principle). Body text stays in the foreground colour, and no fact exists only in colour.
A slide filled with the brand colour is a landmark. Use one for the cover, each section and the closing slide, and keep content slides on the background, where evidence reads best.
## Contrast

**Compute it, never eyeball it.** WCAG 2.2 asks for 4.5:1 for text, and 3:1 for text of 24 px and larger or 18.7 px bold, in both themes. White on a saturated red or orange is often only just above 4.5:1, so text on the brand colour stays large, and secondary text on it at 90% white or more. A brand colour used as text on white needs the same 4.5:1.
Either design the dark theme too, or pin the deck to one theme with `colorScheme` in the frontmatter.
## Checking it
These commands are for you, not for the slides.
1. `pnpm check`, then look at the cover, a section slide and a content slide at full size in `.tmp/export/`.
2. If the deck can switch to dark (<kbd>D</kbd>), `node scripts/export.ts --check --theme dark` after the build, and look again.
3. Put the cover next to the brand's own logo and compare: colour, shape, and the space around the mark.
# Code on slides

The fence options of this deck, the space a slide has for code, and the patterns for the things a talk does with code. The deck's `README.md` has the same option table and wins where the two differ; a change to `plugins/remark-code.ts` updates both.
## Contents
- Fence options
- How much fits
- Walking through code
- Showing a change
- Several files
- Code from real files
- Long code
- Terminal output
- What to cut
## Fence options
Written after the language, in any order:
| Option | Effect |
| `title="src/app.ts"` | Title bar with the file name and a copy button; costs about two lines of height |
| `lineNumbers`, `startLine=10` | Line numbers, from 10; cost four columns |
| `{2,4-6}` | Highlights those lines and dims the rest |
| `{1\|3-4\|all}` | One highlight per step |
| `file="./snippets/app.ts"` | The code of a real file; `#L10-24` for lines, `#name` for a `// #region name` |
| `maxLines=10` | At most that many lines, scrolled to what is highlighted |
| `fold={4-11}`, `fold=#name` | Those lines, or a region of a `file=` snippet, behind one line until a step highlights inside them or a click opens them |
| `diff` | `+` and `-` lines shown as added and removed; `git diff` output works as is |
| `diff split` | The same, starting before and after side by side |
| `diff magic-move` | The diff played from before to after in one step |
| `class="mx-auto w-fit"` | Classes on the frame, never a smaller text size |

A four-backtick `md magic-move` fence holds several fences, one per version. `<CodeTabs>` around several fences makes tabs. Shiki's notation comments mark a line and disappear from the slide: `// [!code ++]`, `// [!code --]`, `// [!code highlight]`, `// [!code focus]`, `// [!code error]`, `// [!code warning]`, `// [!code word:name]`.
## How much fits
Measured on this deck at the 15 px code size, where a character is 9 px wide:
| Where the code is | Columns | With `lineNumbers` |
| Across the slide | 88 | 84 |
| One cell of a two-column `<Columns>` | 39 | 35 |
| The wide cell of `<Columns widths="3:2">` | 48 | 43 |
| The narrow cell of `widths="3:2"` | 30 | 26 |
| The wide cell of `widths="2:1"` | 54 | 49 |
| The narrow cell of `widths="2:1"` | 24 | 20 |
| Above the code | Lines | With `title=` |
| A one-line headline | 13 | 11 |
| A two-line headline | 12 | 10 |

Text above or below the block takes from the same budget. Past these limits the code shrinks to fit, down to 80%, and `pnpm check` warns: shrunk code is under the size a room can read, so treat the warning as a failure. Aim well inside the limits; eight lines and 60 columns read comfortably. Code beside the sentence it proves goes in the wide cell of `<Columns widths="3:2" align="center">`, which centres the sentence level with the code; a narrow cell holds a short config or a list, not a function.
## Walking through code
Highlight steps are the idiom for "look here, now here": one step per sentence you will say, ending on `all` because the print view shows the last step.
````mdx

for (let attempt = 0; ; attempt++) {

return await run()

if (attempt === attempts - 1) throw error
await sleep(100 * 2 ** attempt)
Line numbers only earn their four columns when you will refer to them, and then `startLine=` or `file=` should make them match the real file.
## Showing a change
Never two full listings on consecutive slides: the audience cannot compare what they cannot see at once.
- **`diff`** when the change is the point: pasted `git diff` output works, or code with only the changed lines prefixed.

- **`diff split`** when before and after each need reading as a whole. Each side has half the width: 39 columns, 35 with `lineNumbers`. A `diff` whose lines fit that has a Unified | Split switch on hover, so either view is one click away when someone asks.

- **`diff magic-move`** or a **`md magic-move`** fence when the audience should watch the code evolve: tokens that stay move, the rest fade, new text is marked. Each version is a step, and a version's own `{…}` highlights add steps after it.

```ts

return "Hello, " + name

return `Hello, ${name}!`
## Several files

`<CodeTabs>` shows fences as tabs, one at a time, and plays their highlight steps in order. Use it when the talk moves between files that belong together, such as a component and its test. The print view shows only the tab of the last step, so the slide's headline must not depend on the other tabs.
## Code from real files

`file="./snippets/counter.ts#increment"` reads the lines between `// #region increment` and `// #endregion` in that file, leaving the markers out; `#L10-24` reads lines. The path is relative to the `.mdx` file. Code in `snippets/` is compiled by `pnpm typecheck`, so the slides cannot show code that no longer compiles, and the slide updates when the file changes. Prefer a region to line numbers: regions survive edits above them.
## Long code
Past the limits, pick in this order:
1. **Cut** to the lines that make the point, with `// …` where code was left out.

2. **Fold** what is not the point with `fold={4-11}`, when the code must stay whole or the audience should see that something is there: each fold costs one line, an arrow and `8 lines`, which stays while the fold is open. A step that highlights inside a fold opens it and the next step shuts it, so the block must also fit while it is open, that line included; `pnpm check` renders every step.
3. **Split** across slides, one idea each.

4. **`maxLines=`** when the audience needs to see that the code is long, or where it sits: the block stays that tall and scrolls to each highlight. The print view shows only its first lines, so the headline must not depend on the rest.
## Terminal output

Show only the lines that prove the point, in a `text` or `sh` fence with a `title=` naming the command. Cut timestamps, absolute paths and progress bars, and mark the line that matters with `// [!code highlight]`. Never a scrolling log; a recorded demo is not a slide.
## What to cut

Nobody compiles a slide. Imports, types the audience already knows, error handling and logging go unless they are the point, and the notes say what was cut when it matters. Rename to the words the talk uses. When code on a slide would not compile as shown, the notes say so.
# How decks fail

Each entry gives the failure, a test that finds it, and the fix. Tests marked "source" run on `slides.mdx`; "render" ones on the images `pnpm check` writes to `.tmp/export/`, where every slide is fully revealed. A content slide is any slide that is not a `<Cover>`, `<Section>`, `<Statement>` or `<Quote>`.
## Contents
- The talk
- Headlines
- Bodies
- Builds
- Code
- Legibility
- Content
- MDX
## The talk

**No big idea.** Failure: the slides are about a topic but argue nothing. Test: state the talk's point in one sentence from the headlines alone; if you cannot, it fails. Fix: write the sentence, then cut or rewrite every slide that does not support it.

**Agenda first.** Failure: slide 2 is "Agenda", "Outline" or "Overview", before the problem is stated. Test (source): the second slide's `##` matches `agenda|outline|overview|contents`. Fix: open with the problem and the promise; a roadmap, if any, comes after them with at most four parts.

**Weak ending.** Failure: the last slide is "Questions?", "Thank you" or "The end", which is what stays on screen longest. Test (source): the last content slide's headline. Fix: a takeaway slide restating the big idea, left up for questions.
**Too many slides for the slot.** Failure: more content slides than minutes. Test (source): count `---` separated content slides against the stated length. Fix: cut ideas, not the time per idea.
## Headlines

**Topic label.** Failure: `## Results`, `## Architecture`, `## Background`. Test (source): a `##` with fewer than four words, no verb, or one of the usual labels. Fix: the sentence the slide proves, `## Caching cut p99 latency from 800 ms to 120 ms`.

**Question headline.** Failure: `## Why is it slow?` with the answer only spoken. Test (source): a `##` ending in `?` with no later step revealing the answer. Fix: state the answer; or keep the question and reveal the answer as a `<Step>`.

**Headline past two lines.** Failure: the eye has to read a paragraph before the slide. Test (render): the headline wraps to three lines; in source, over about 90 characters at `##`. Fix: say less, and move the qualification to the notes.
**Headlines that do not add up.** Failure: each slide is fine, but in order they wander. Test: read every `##` in order as a paragraph. Fix: reorder, merge, or cut until they make the argument.
## Bodies

**Wall of bullets.** Failure: a headline and a list, the most common slide there is. Test (source): a content slide whose body is only a list, or any list over four items. Fix: find the evidence behind the list, a diagram, code, a number or a comparison, and move the items to the notes.

**Slideument.** Failure: paragraphs of prose on the canvas. Test (render): more than about 33 words on a content slide, or a paragraph over two lines. Fix: keep the claim and its evidence; the prose goes to `<Notes>`.

**Script on the slide.** Failure: the notes and the slide say the same sentences, so the audience reads ahead. Test (source): a sentence of a slide's `<Notes>` appears on the slide. Fix: the slide shows, the notes say.
**Two ideas on one slide.** Failure: two headlines' worth of content under one. Test: the headline needs "and" to cover the body. Fix: two slides.

**Comparison across slides.** Failure: "before" on one slide and "after" on the next. Test (source): consecutive slides whose code or tables share most of their lines. Fix: one slide with `<Columns>`, a `diff`, `diff split` or a magic move.
**Distant labels.** Failure: a legend, a key, or "see left", "as shown below". Test (render and source): a legend on a chart, or those phrases in the text. Fix: label the thing itself.
## Builds

**Drip-fed text.** Failure: every bullet revealed one by one, for no reason. Test (source): `<Steps>` around more than four text items, or on every slide. Fix: show them at once, or replace the list; keep builds for parts of a graphic or code and for a punch line.

**Unfinished last step.** Failure: the printed slide shows the middle of a build: dimmed code, the wrong magic-move version. Test (source): a `{…|…}` highlight sequence that does not end in `all`; the last version of a magic move is not the one worth printing. Fix: end on `all`, or reorder the versions.
## Code

**Code too big.** Failure: `pnpm check` warns that code was shrunk to fit, or fails because it runs out of its frame. Test (render): the warning; in source, a line over 88 columns (39 in a column, 48 in the wide cell of `widths="3:2"`) or a block over 13 lines. Fix: cut to the point, split, or `maxLines=`; never a smaller font.

**Noise.** Failure: imports, boilerplate and error handling around the three lines that matter. Test (source): a code slide starting with `import` lines that the talk never mentions. Fix: cut them, and mark gaps with `// …`.
**Two full listings.** Failure: the old and new code as two blocks. Test (source): two fences on a slide, or on consecutive slides, that mostly match. Fix: a `diff` or a magic move.

**Diagram too big.** Failure: node labels too small to read from the back, or a diagram squeezed into a column. Test (render): `pnpm check` warns that the diagram was shrunk to fit, or the build warns that it is too wide. Fix: fewer nodes, shorter labels, one direction, or the diagram on a slide of its own.

**Terminal dump.** Failure: a screenful of log or command output. Test (source): a `text`, `sh` or `console` fence over about eight lines. Fix: keep the lines that prove the point and highlight the one that matters.

**Code headline that describes.** Failure: `## The retry function`. Test (source): a code slide whose `##` names the code instead of saying what it does or proves. Fix: `## retry waits longer after every failure`.
## Legibility
**Small text.** Failure: content under 18 px, or code under 15 px. Test (source): `text-sm`, `text-xs`, `text-[…px]` under 18 on content, or `class="text-sm"` on a fence. Fix: say less, or split.

**Faint text.** Failure: content in a muted colour at reduced opacity. Test (source): `text-muted-foreground/70` or any `/50`, `/60`, `/70` on content. Fix: `text-muted-foreground` at full strength, or the foreground.
**Colour carries the meaning.** Failure: "the red ones failed", with nothing else marking them. Test: look at the slide in greyscale. Fix: a label or a shape as well as the colour.

**Hidden overflow.** Failure: a slide made to pass by clipping or scaling it. Test (source): `overflow-hidden`, `max-h-`, `scale-`, `zoom` or `leading-none` added in `slides.mdx`. Fix: remove it and split the slide.
## Content

**Invented numbers.** Failure: a statistic, date, version or quotation the user never gave. Test: each figure on a slide appears in the user's material, and its source is in the slide's notes. Fix: ask for the number, or cut the claim.

**Placeholders.** Failure: "Lorem ipsum", "TODO", "[insert chart]", "Option A". Test (source): search the visible text for `lorem|ipsum|TODO|TBD|FIXME|\[insert|placeholder|xxx`. Fix: real content, or no slide.

**Chatbot tells.** Failure: an emoji before headings or bullets, Title Case Headlines, a "Key takeaways" slide, bullets that open with a bold phrase and a colon. Test (source): those patterns. Fix: a sentence headline and plain text.
## MDX
**A deck that renders nothing.** Failure: one slide's mistake blanks the whole deck in the browser. Test: `pnpm check` fails with a page error or a compile error. Fix, by cause:
- `{word}` in prose is a JavaScript expression: write `\{word\}` or put it in inline code.
- `<!-- comment -->` does not parse: write `{/* comment */}`.
- `<` before a digit does not parse: write "under 100 ms".

- `
` must be `
`, and `` must be `[text](https://…)`.

**Markdown that stays inline.** Failure: a list or several paragraphs inside a component run together on one line, dashes and all. Test (render): list dashes or run-on paragraphs on the slide; in source, block Markdown on the same line as a component's tags. Fix: blank lines between the component's tags and the Markdown inside.

**A split that does not split.** Failure: two columns run together in one, or two slides show as one, and a line of text became a heading. Test (source): a `---` right under a line of text with no blank line between, which the build reports as `"---" right under "…" makes it a heading`; or `<Columns widths>` naming more or fewer widths than its `---` make columns, which it reports too. Fix: a blank line above every `---`, and one width per column.
# Structuring a talk

How a talk is put together before any slide is written. There is no experimental literature on talk structure, only the advice of people who give and judge many talks; the rules below say whose advice each one is, so a user's own convention can win where it differs.
## Contents
- The big idea
- Opening
- The arc
- Signposts
- Closing
- Timing
- Rehearsal
- An outline to start from
## The big idea

Write the big idea as one sentence with a verb and a stake before anything else: "If the audience remembers only one thing from your talk, what should it be?" (Peyton Jones). Duarte asks for a complete sentence, because a noun and a verb force a position, and for what is at stake if the audience ignores it. "Caching" is a topic; "Caching our read path would let one database serve ten times the traffic" is a big idea.
Every slide must support it. Prune the rest, however true: "narrow and deep beats wide and shallow" (Peyton Jones). When time is short, keep the example and drop the general case.
## Opening
The audience decides in the first two minutes whether to listen (Peyton Jones). Spend them on:
- **The problem**, concrete: an incident, a number, a piece of code that hurts.
- **The promise**: what the audience will know or be able to do at the end that they cannot now (Winston's "empowerment promise"; PyCon asks the same of every proposal).

Not an agenda, not a biography, not a joke unrelated to the talk. An outline shown before the motivation "conveys near zero information" (Peyton Jones); once the problem is on the table, a roadmap of at most four parts can orient the audience.
## The arc

Alternate what is and what could be, then call the audience to act (Duarte, *Resonate*). For a technical talk the Heilmeier questions make a checklist: what are you trying to do, how is it done today and what limits it, what is new in your approach, who cares, and how will you know it worked.
Put a concrete example next to every abstract claim: code, data, a trace, a screenshot. "Examples are your main weapon" (Peyton Jones).
## Signposts

Mark the seams: a `<Section>` slide where the talk turns, named after the part of the roadmap it starts (Kosslyn; Winston's "verbal punctuation"). The names are claims or questions the section answers, never "Introduction", "Background" or "Conclusion".
Repeat the big idea about three times: in the opening, at the midpoint, perhaps as a `<Statement>`, and on the last slide. Some of the room was not listening the first time (Winston).
## Closing

The last slide restates the takeaway, the contributions or the call to action as sentences, and stays on screen through the questions (Winston; Alley). Not "Questions?", "Thank you" or "The end": the slide on screen the longest should be the one worth remembering. Credit collaborators on the first slide, not the last. Backup slides for expected questions go after it, as `<Slide hidden>` drafts or after the closing slide.
## Timing

Plan about one content slide per minute, and aim for 80% of the slot: "if they give you an hour, target forty minutes" (Duarte). Alley and Neeley ask for at least a minute a slide; their own study ran 44 seconds a slide, so treat it as a planning figure, not a law. Count a slide once however many steps it has. Finish on time, always (Peyton Jones).
Put a time budget per section in the first slide's `<Notes>`, so the presenter view shows it.
## Rehearsal

You cannot rehearse for the user, so say what to do: one timed run out loud, noting where they stall or run long, then cut or split those slides (Schlawack's loop: practise out loud, take notes, fix the slides, repeat). A first run often takes more than twice the slot (Schlawack). The notes should be cues the speaker glances at, with the first few sentences of the talk written out in full.
## An outline to start from
Adjust it to the talk; it is a shape, not a form.
1. `<Cover>`: the title, as the big idea or a promise, and who is speaking.
2. The problem, concrete, with evidence.
3. The promise: what the audience will leave with.
4. Optional roadmap: at most four parts, a sentence headline.
5. One `<Section>` per part, each with its slides: claim, evidence, example.
6. A `<Statement>` restating the big idea at the midpoint of a long talk.
7. The takeaway slide, left up for questions.
